title: How Lobbying Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how lobbying works, starting with the constitutional right to petition government and the bad reputation lobbyists have had since at least the 1600s and 1800s. They cover historical scandals (Jack Abramoff, the Bank of the United States and Daniel Webster's letter, the Credit Mobilier scandal of the Gilded Age, Sam Ward's social lobbying), the origin of the word "lobby," and the 1876 and 1995/2007 registration and disclosure laws and their loopholes. They describe direct, indirect (social) and grassroots lobbying, the revolving door between Congress and K Street, and how cuts to congressional staff and research agencies under Newt Gingrich and earlier increased reliance on lobbyists. They discuss lobbying spending figures, rent seeking such as fossil fuel subsidies, and proposals from Drutman and Teles's Washington Monthly article to increase congressional staff salaries. The episode closes with listener mail from Colin about listening to old episodes in reverse order.
topics: Honest Leadership and Open Government Act

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about recording without a producer and decide to do an episode on lobbying, noting lobbyists' feedback.

segments.title: Lobbying's bad reputation and Jack Abramoff
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why lobbyists are widely distrusted, using Jack Abramoff's bribery and fraud as an example, and his prison sentence and restitution.

segments.title: Early criticism and the constitutional right to petition
segments.summary: They read Emily Edson Briggs's 1869 column 'The Dragons of the Lobby' and explain that lobbying is protected by the First Amendment's right to petition, though corporate interests exploited it. Kennedy's view that lobbyists explain complex issues to legislators is also cited.

segments.title: Why legislators depend on lobbyists
segments.summary: Lawmakers need to make names through passing bills but lack time and staff to write legislation, so they turn to lobbyists, whose slanted input shapes laws.

segments.title: Lobbying and fundraising
segments.summary: Lobbyists act as major fundraisers for the politicians they lobby, which the hosts describe as part of why lobbying is pernicious. Hosts also note the lobbying spending amounts in 2014 and registered lobbyist counts.

segments.title: Origin of the word lobby and early lobbying
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the popular story that the word 'lobby' came from the Willard Hotel and Ulysses Grant, then trace the term to 1640s England's House of Commons lobby. They describe early American lobbying around the first Congress and the tariff act.

segments.title: Bank of the United States and Daniel Webster
segments.summary: The Bank of the United States is described as an early corrupt organization that paid board members in Congress. Daniel Webster's letter to the bank about his unrenewed retainer is recounted.

segments.title: Gilded Age scandals: Credit Mobilier and Sam Ward
segments.summary: The Credit Mobilier scandal is described: Union Pacific insiders inflated stock and gave shares to Congress members as bribes for land grants. Sam Ward is described as the father of social lobbying through parties and dinners. K Street is explained as the lobbying hub.

segments.title: Mid-century regulation and the revolving door
segments.summary: After the Gilded Age, lobbying waned, then Congress set rules in the 1940s because staffers were leaving for K Street. Business shifted to active lobbying in the 1970s and 80s, and lobbying grew rapidly with corporate subsidies.

segments.title: Lobbying spending by corporations and top spenders
segments.summary: Northrop Grumman's lobbying spending is compared with its contract wins, and open secrets data lists the top 2014 lobbying spenders including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Blue Cross Blue Shield and Google. Gingrich's 1990s cuts to congressional staff are also discussed.

segments.title: Rent seeking, the revolving door and lobbying regulation
segments.summary: The hosts explain rent seeking through fossil fuel subsidies and discuss the revolving door, including former legislators and officials who went to lobbying firms. They also describe the 2007 lobbying-registration rules and their loopholes, including the time-based threshold.

segments.title: Types of lobbying and reform proposals
segments.summary: Direct, indirect (social), and grassroots lobbying are explained. The hosts discuss the Washington Monthly article's proposals to increase congressional staff salaries and research capacity, and the value of the CBO.

segments.title: Listener mail from Colin on binge listening
segments.summary: Colin suggests listening to the archive from newest to oldest. Josh and Chuck respond and mention possible future episode redos.
